slides.title: PermitFlow: how it is built
slides.lead: Scope, architecture, the decisions that make the brief's guarantees true, the pipeline, the evidence, and the gaps. Every claim names its file.
slides.notes: This is the technical half of the debrief. The pitch deck showed the product; this deck shows how it is built and why. I will go in the order the brief evaluates: scope judgement, then the architecture and four decisions, then production readiness through the pipeline and the test evidence, then how I used AI, then what I would do next. Every slide names the file a reviewer can open.

slides.title: Three use cases, one status table, five things being evaluated.
cases: Form with sections, drag-and-drop uploads, live AI status per document, progress, feedback on top, edit only flagged parts, unlimited rounds, history.
Full submission, AI results, contextual feedback with templates, status change notifies, changed sections highlighted, compare revisions, resolution tracked, audit trail.
The three post-site statuses and their transitions exist and are tested; the checklist model and screens are not built. Recorded in SCOPE.md with what production needs.
slides.table: Status table: 12 internal statuses with a different label per role. Implemented as data in domain/labels.py, verbatim from the brief, plus draft and withdrawn as written assumptions.
areas: docs/README.md is the index; docs/reviews/ASSESSMENT_TRACEABILITY.md maps every brief line to code, test and evidence
slides.notes: The brief gives three use cases and says two is fine. It also gives a status table with different labels per role, and it lists five evaluation areas. I built use cases one and two in full because they are one loop: submit, review, feedback, resubmit, compare. Use case three is deferred, but the state machine already holds its statuses, so adding it is additive, not a rewrite. The status table is data in the code, not prose. The deck follows the five evaluation areas in order, and the traceability document maps every checkable line of the brief to where it is implemented and tested.

slides.title: Where the brief was ambiguous, the assumption is written down and enforced by code.
items: A draft state exists before Application Received
Needed for save and return; never shown to officers; deletable outright until submitted (US-045). SCOPE.md assumption 2 and 14.
Under Review starts on an explicit officer action
So the actor lands in the audit trail. Start review is a transition row, not a side effect. Assumption 3.
Requesting resubmission needs at least one open feedback item
Guard on the transition; the button is disabled with the reason. Assumption 4, domain/workflow.py.
Addressed is automatic, resolved is a decision
The linked section or document changed in the next revision: addressed. The officer confirms: resolved. Assumption 7.
Only flagged sections may change on resubmission: enforced
The API returns 403 for any other change. A product decision open to reversal. Assumption 13, domain/resolution.py.
Operators see Pending Approval as a waiting state
The brief's own table gives that label; the officer-only label Route to Approval and the decision note never reach an operator. Assumption 17.
slides.foot: All 17 assumptions: SCOPE.md. Each one that changes behaviour has a test.
slides.notes: Six of the seventeen assumptions, the ones that changed behaviour. The brief's table starts at Application Received, so a draft state is an assumption. The brief does not say who moves a case to Under Review, so I made it an officer action, which puts an actor in the audit trail. Requesting resubmission with no feedback would strand the operator, so it is guarded. Addressed versus resolved separates what the system can know from what the officer decides. Only flagged sections is enforced at the API, not suggested. And the approval stage: the brief's constraints say operators never see it, while the brief's own table gives operators a Pending Approval label; I followed the table and the spirit, no internal code and no officer-only label ever reaches an operator.

slides.title: A modular monolith: one API in strict layers, one web app, one database, an isolated AI module.
callouts: Layers, enforced
api, services, domain, repositories, models. domain is pure Python: no SQLAlchemy, no FastAPI, no I/O. tests/unit/test_layering.py fails the build if a layer imports downward the wrong way. ADR-001.
PostgreSQL only
Relations for users, applications, feedback and audit; every submitted revision an immutable JSON snapshot. Row locks and a version column for concurrency. ADR-002.
AI in-process, behind an interface
Background task per document, result polled every 2 s, stale runs marked failed on restart. VerificationProvider with OpenAI and a deterministic mock. ADR-004, the worker is next.
Stack
FastAPI, SQLAlchemy 2, Pydantic v2, Alembic; React 19, TypeScript strict, Vite, TanStack Query, React Hook Form, Zod; pytest, vitest, Playwright. ADR-009.
slides.foot: docs/architecture/ARCHITECTURE.md (API table, request flows) · docs/architecture/decisions (12 ADRs, three groups: shape, rules, delivery)
slides.notes: The shape. One FastAPI backend in five layers with a test that enforces the direction of imports; the domain layer is pure Python and is the code a reviewer should read first: the state machine, the labels, the diff, the editability rules. One React app that calls the API directly. One PostgreSQL with relational tables plus a JSON snapshot per revision. Files on a volume behind a storage interface. The AI verifier is a module with one caller, services.verification, and one interface, so it can move to a worker or another provider without touching the rest. Twelve ADRs in three groups; the next four slides are the rules that make the brief's guarantees true.

slides.title: The workflow is a table, not a set of if statements.
slides.chose: The fourteen statuses and every allowed move as data: from, to, actor, guard, label. One function, transition(), consults it. available_actions() gives the UI its buttons with the reason a button is disabled.
slides.over: Status changes scattered through services, or a workflow library with its own model of the world.
slides.because: A table can be compared with the brief's status table line by line and tested exhaustively. Adding a status is a row. Reject is possible from every non-terminal post-submission state, so no case can get stuck.
evidence: 18 transition rows plus withdraw from any post-submission state; guards: is_complete, open_feedback_count, has_changes_to_flagged_targets
the brief's table verbatim: internal status, officer label, operator label, badge tone
every (source, target, actor) combination: 14 x 14 x 3 = 588 cases; terminal states have no exits; guards
row lock, expected_version, 409 invalid_transition with the allowed list, audit and notification in the same transaction
slides.tradeoff: Guards are Python callables, so a guard that needs data the context does not carry means extending the context. Accepted: the context has three fields and has not grown since Day 1.
slides.notes: Decision one. The brief's status table has to hold exactly, with a different label per role. So the workflow is data: a tuple of transition rows, each with the source, the target, the actor, an optional guard and the label the button shows. One function consults it, and it is the only way status changes. The test iterates every combination of source, target and actor, 588 cases, and asserts that only the listed rows pass. The labels file is the brief's table typed in, and a test compares it. Reject from every post-submission state is deliberate: the brief says no application is lost, and a case that cannot move is a lost case.

slides.title: Operators never see internal status codes, because the API cannot send them.
slides.chose: Role checked per router; ownership enforced in the one function that loads an application (another owner's case is a 404, not a 403); a separate response model per role, so the operator view has no field for the internal status or the officer label.
slides.over: Checking roles in the UI, or one shared response shape with fields hidden client-side.
slides.because: The brief's constraint, operators cannot see the approval stage, becomes a property of the types and the tests, not a hope. A leaked field would be a schema change, which a reviewer sees in the diff.
evidence: get_for(user, id) applies the operator_id filter; NotFound for another owner
operator view: operator label, released feedback without author, no internal status, no decision note before the outcome
an authorization test for every endpoint: wrong role 403, wrong owner 404, cross-application ids 404, admin read-only
slides.tradeoff: Two response models to keep in step when a field is added. Accepted: the layering test and the API table in ARCHITECTURE.md make a missed field visible.
slides.notes: Decision two is the brief's hardest constraint: operators must never see the internal approval stage. The usual answer is to hide it in the UI. Here the operator response model does not have the field. Role is checked per router, ownership is checked in the one function that loads an application, and another owner's application is a 404 so the id space leaks nothing. Every endpoint has an authorization test: wrong role, wrong owner, an id from another application. Admin is read-only by construction: it has no transitions.

slides.title: The AI check advises. Strict schemas and deterministic rules decide what an answer is allowed to mean.
slides.chose: A provider interface with two implementations (OpenAI structured output, deterministic mock). A pinned wire schema, then a strict domain model (extra forbidden, confidence 0 to 1, status must agree with the issue list), then rules after the model: confidence under 0.6 or an injection phrase forces needs_review. The result is stored on the run and shown to the officer. It never touches status, feedback or editability.
slides.over: Letting the model's answer drive the workflow, or free-text answers parsed by hand.
slides.because: The brief says AI assists and the officer decides. With strict schemas a bad answer becomes a flagged answer, never a state change. Over quota or on failure the run is stored unavailable and the application proceeds.
evidence: VerificationProvider; prompt_version 2026-09-19.3 stamped on every run; 30 s timeout, one retry
the only caller of infra.ai; own session and transaction; text extraction capped (30 pages, 20 000 chars, 10 s); never raises out of the task
evals/: 14 golden cases, 2 injection cases, 21 fairness runs
mock gate on every push, live nightly, LangSmith experiment per run; docs/ai/AI_ASSURANCE.md
slides.tradeoff: Confidence is the model's own estimate and is uncalibrated; the injection heuristic is English-only phrases. Both recorded as next steps with the tools to fix them.
slides.notes: Decision three. The model sees the extracted text and the form section and returns a structured answer through a pinned wire schema. That answer is validated into a strict domain model: unknown fields are rejected, confidence is bounded, and the status must agree with the issue list whatever the model said. Then deterministic rules run: low confidence or an instruction-like phrase in the document forces needs review. The result goes on the verification run and into the officer's view with its evidence. It never changes status. If the provider fails, times out, or the daily quota is spent, the run is stored unavailable and the application proceeds; the check is advisory, so refusing a model call is always safe. Every prompt change is gated by fourteen golden cases and twenty-one name-swap fairness runs.

slides.title: Nothing is lost between rounds: every submission is a frozen snapshot, and every change writes its audit row in the same transaction.
slides.chose: Each submit or resubmit stores Revision N: the form as JSON plus the document ids. The comparison between revisions is computed at read time from the snapshots. Audit events, notifications and the licence on approval are written in the same database transaction as the change; there is no update or delete path for audit rows.
slides.over: Editing one mutable record, storing diffs instead of snapshots, or a separate logging pipeline and database triggers.
slides.because: Never lost between rounds and complete audit trail become true by construction. The officer's compare view cannot disagree with what was submitted. A change without its audit row cannot exist, and vice versa.
evidence: immutable rows; raised_in_revision on feedback; sha256 on documents so an identical re-upload is no change
field-level form diff and document add, remove, replace; GET /applications/{id}/compare?from=n&to=m
SELECT FOR UPDATE, only flagged targets may change (403), at least one flagged target changed (422), Revision N+1, feedback to addressed, audit, notify, one commit
actor, role, plain-language summary from domain/audit_labels.py, payload, chronological; 748 backend tests include every event type
slides.tradeoff: Snapshots grow with rounds; at this form size a revision is a few kilobytes. A separate audit store would be the answer at a scale this product is not at.
slides.notes: Decision four covers two ADRs because they are one promise. Every submission is a frozen snapshot of the form and the document ids; the diff the officer sees is computed from two snapshots when asked, so it can never disagree with what was submitted. The resubmission path locks the row, checks that only flagged targets changed, requires at least one of them to have changed, writes the new revision, marks feedback addressed, writes the audit rows and the notifications, and commits once. Audit rows have no update or delete path in the code. The audit endpoint shows actor, role, a plain-language summary and the payload, in order.

slides.title: Build once, promote by tag, production behind a person.
callouts: Images built once
CI builds both images after every other job is green and pushes them to GHCR with sha-<commit>, the branch, and v0.3.0 on main. Railway never builds; the tested artefact is the deployed artefact.
Two environments, nothing shared
development from dev, production from main. Own PostgreSQL 18, own uploads volume, own secrets, own tokens, own domains.
Gates
Production waits for the repository owner's approval in the GitHub environment. Both environments gate on /api/v1/health, /healthz and config.js naming the right API. Rollback is the previous tag.
Known limit

A workflow_run job executes on the default branch, dev, and the production environment admits only main, so production is deployed by hand: gh workflow run deploy.yml --ref main. Documented in OPERATIONS.md.
slides.foot: docs/operations/OPERATIONS.md: shape, secrets and variables, seeding, custom domain, rollback, what was verified
slides.notes: Delivery. CI builds the two Docker images once and pushes them to the GitHub registry with three tags: the commit, the branch, and the version on main. Railway pulls by tag and never builds, so what was tested is what runs. Two environments that share nothing. Production waits for a person, me, to approve the job in GitHub, and both environments gate on health and on the frontend naming the right API. One limit found at the release: the automatic production job is rejected by GitHub's branch policy because workflow_run executes on the default branch, so production is dispatched by hand with the same approval and gates. It is written down rather than worked around.

slides.title: Seven CI jobs, an AI gate with six, a live evaluation, and a deploy that waits for health.
callouts: Everything blocks

Backend (ruff, mypy strict, 748 pytest on PostgreSQL), Frontend (eslint, tsc, 152 vitest with thresholds, build), gitleaks, pip-audit, bandit, npm audit, End to end (the whole stack in the runner, Playwright), Images. No job is advisory.
AI gate on every push
Model approval, contracts on a real database, 14 golden cases, adversarial injection cases, 21 fairness runs, verdict. On the mock provider so it is deterministic and free.
Live evaluation
Nightly and on AI-path pushes against the real OpenAI model: blocking at 14 of 14, each run recorded as a LangSmith experiment. Fails loudly when the key is missing.
Reproducible
The end-to-end job runs migrations, seed, uvicorn and vite preview inside the runner, with rate limits set to 0 and the mock provider. The same commands run locally.
slides.foot: .github/workflows: ci.yml, ai-gate.yml (workflow_call), ai-eval.yml, deploy.yml · shell: bash with pipefail everywhere
slides.notes: CI. Seven jobs, all blocking, and the image job waits for every one of them. The AI gate is a reusable workflow called by CI: model approval, contract tests on a real database, the golden set, the adversarial cases, the fairness check, and a verdict; on the mock provider so it is deterministic. The live evaluation is a separate workflow because it costs money and needs a key: nightly and whenever the AI module or the set changes, blocking at fourteen of fourteen, each run a LangSmith experiment. One lesson from the last day: the contracts job passed falsely once because a pipe masked the exit code; every workflow now runs with pipefail and the job greps for the word passed.

slides.title: Checked by tests, gates and a written record.
checks: Pydantic 422 with per-field details; upload allowlist, size streamed to 10 MB, magic bytes; zod schemas built from the server's form schema.
{ error: { code, message, details } } on every route, including 401, 403, 422, 429 and 500 with a request id and no stack trace.
SELECT FOR UPDATE on the application; expected_version on transitions (409 version_conflict); stale AI runs recovered on restart.
240 requests and 20 sign-ins per client per minute with Retry-After; 20 open drafts; 60 checks per applicant and 1 000 per day, over quota stored unavailable.
CSP, HSTS, COOP, Permissions-Policy on both tiers; Argon2, JWT 8 h re-validated per request; gitleaks over the history; .env.example documents every variable.
axe gate in CI over 23 screen states; labels never colour alone; policy pages and demonstration notices; fonts self-hosted.
reviews: docs/security/THREAT_MODEL.md: T1 to T22 plus T1a, STRIDE per asset, the control for each, what is accepted for a demonstration and why.
docs/reviews/PRODUCTION_READINESS_REVIEW.md: 20 rows, severity, what mitigates today, what production needs.
docs/security/SECURITY_REVIEW.md: four attack scenarios walked through against the code, with the fix or the accepted risk.
docs/uat/UAT_PLAN.md: twelve scripts, executed on development and again on production after v0.3.0.
slides.notes: Production readiness as evidence rather than adjectives. Seven hundred and forty-eight backend tests on a real PostgreSQL, a hundred and fifty-two frontend tests with coverage thresholds that fail the build, eight Playwright specs including an accessibility gate over twenty-three screen states. Validation at every boundary, one error shape everywhere, row locks and a version column, abuse limits with quotas counted where the truth lives. [Next] And the written record: a threat model with a control per threat, a readiness review with severity per row, a security review that walks four attack scenarios, and a UAT plan executed twice. Where something is accepted for a demonstration, the document says so and says what production needs.

slides.title: AI wrote most of the code. The rules it worked under, and the checks on its output, are in the repository.

rows: Claude Code (Opus 5, some Fable 5.1) in Cursor's terminal; Cursor to read every diff before a commit; Wispr Flow to dictate the long briefs; Claude in Chrome for the dashboard steps and persona run-throughs; Notion, Railway, GitHub through MCP and CLIs.

Two instruction files: a global engineering standard and the checked-in CLAUDE.md (three personas, layering, every status change through workflow.py, AI never mutates state, same-transaction audit, error envelope, the per-story checklist). The brief's five context types, each with an example in AI_USAGE.md.

Full suites on every story; browser checks at 390, 1024 and 1280; subagent reviews with separate briefs (design critique, edge cases, bug hunts, a strict assessor); every finding reproduced before a fix; docs checked against code at each sprint close.

Invented enum values and a valid verdict on an expired certificate (pinned schema, date in the prompt); a scope-creeping story and a red landing band (rejected); a transition the state machine did not allow (became Return to review); a scratch file swept into a commit.

brag (launch video workflow); the HyperFrames set: hyperframes-core, -animation, -keyframes, -cli, -audio, media-use, general-video, slideshow; demo-video (Playwright footage recipe); claude-video-generator (narrated walkthrough rules).

Playwright records the development environment at 1920 x 1080 with a drawn cursor; narration through Kokoro via hyperframes tts; music from the HeyGen catalogue with my own sign-in; a HyperFrames composition checked and rendered at 60 fps.

Plans reviewed by four persona subagents through fourteen revisions before any build; the code, not the design documents, as the source of truth; a leak sweep of every recording for emails and ids; footage on development, never production.

ChatGPT image generation from prompts written against the workflows and docs; each picture rated against the code before use; two rejected for invented components (a CDN, an Azure tenant, a proxying frontend).

slides.foot: README.md AI Usage (short) · AI_USAGE.md (full record: verbatim prompts, discarded output, who did what)
slides.notes: How AI was used, honestly. Claude Code wrote most of the code and the documents, inside two instruction files that are in the repository, so the rules it followed are reviewable. I read every diff in Cursor before a commit and pushed only on an explicit yes. Output was checked by the suites, by browser checks at three widths, by subagent reviews with separate briefs, and by a strict assessor pass on the last day. The list of where it was wrong is in the README. The debrief material came from a second session with Claude Code skills for video: brag for the launch video, the HyperFrames set for composition and rendering, demo-video for the footage, and claude-video-generator for the narrated walkthrough. The diagrams in this deck were generated by ChatGPT from prompts I wrote against the code, and each was rated before use; two were rejected because they invented a CDN and an Azure tenant.

slides.title: Known gaps first, then what production would need.
items: Use case 3
The checklist model, the officer capture screen with draft save, per-item clarification and the operator's targeted response. The statuses and transitions exist. About 1.5 days.
A worker for the AI checks
Redis and a worker, or a Postgres SKIP LOCKED queue, so checks survive deploys and scale apart from the API. ADR-004 has one call site to change.
Object storage and backups
S3-compatible bucket with signed URLs and a virus scan; a file backup and a restore drill; a retention policy for documents and traces.
Session and edge
httpOnly cookie with CSRF protection instead of sessionStorage; CSP nonces; the rate windows in Redis or at the edge.
AI assurance

A labelled set from officer overrides; promptfoo or PyRIT red-team beyond two injection cases; Project Moonshot for Singapore evidence; calibrated confidence; in-region tracing; a multilingual injection classifier.
Admin epic, v0.4.0
Overview with AI health and quota counters, audit feed, read-only case view, user management. Role and routes reserved, screens not built.
Delivery
Staging with a copy of production data for migration rehearsal; two replicas; Semgrep and CodeQL; Trivy with an SBOM on the images.
Product
Email delivery, officer assignment, more licence types via a configurable form schema, a public verification page for certificates.

slides.notes: Known gaps first. Use case three is the largest functional gap and the first thing to schedule; the state machine already holds it. Then the worker for the AI checks, object storage with backups, and the session and edge hardening that a demonstration accepted. AI assurance has a specific list: a labelled set grown from officer overrides, a red-team suite, Project Moonshot for the Singapore evidence, calibrated confidence, in-region tracing. The admin epic is scoped on the board as v0.4.0. Delivery wants staging, replicas and image scanning. Each item has a row with severity in the readiness review.

slides.title: Every decision has a file. Every claim has a test.
slides.line: Thank you. Questions on any file, any decision, any gap.
slides.notes: That is the technical account. Scope written before code and re-read at each close; four decisions that turn the brief's guarantees into properties of the code; a pipeline that deploys only what it tested; evidence in tests and in documents that say what is accepted and why. I am happy to open any file.
